questoes.pergunta:
SCENARIO — Pomar Pagamentos is a fintech in Porto Alegre that processes card payments for small retailers. The backend is a .NET 8 monorepo (40 projects, ~600,000 lines) with an Angular front end, maintained by 40 developers in 6 squads. The company has adopted Claude Code to generate and refactor code. Constraints: the card encryption code is in PCI-DSS scope and cannot be changed without review by the security team; architecture conventions must apply equally to all devs; and context cost must be kept under control, because sessions are long.

Problem: the tech lead wrote the convention "in the domain layer, return Result<T> instead of throwing exceptions" in the ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file on his own machine. In his sessions, Claude follows the rule; in those of the other 39 devs, it does not. What is the most appropriate fix?
opcoes: Ask each dev to copy the convention into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, with a checklist item in onboarding.
Move the convention to a CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root.
Move the convention to the project CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md) and version it in the repository.
Ask the platform team to publish the convention as a managed policy (an organization-managed CLAUDE.md).
questoes.explicacao: CLAUDE.md hierarchy: user (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) is personal; project (./CLAUDE.md) belongs to the team and is versioned; CLAUDE.local.md is personal and gitignored; managed policy belongs to the organization. A repository convention that applies to everyone → project CLAUDE.md.
feedbacks: Tempting because it replicates what already works for the tech lead. But the user file is personal and not versioned: the copies drift over time and new devs end up without the rule. A team convention belongs in the repository.
Tempting because the name sounds like a "project file". But CLAUDE.local.md is personal and stays out of git (gitignored): it still applies only to whoever created it.
Correct. The project CLAUDE.md is versioned and shared: every dev who clones the monorepo gets the same instruction, and changes go through review like any other code.

Tempting because it guarantees full reach. But this is an architecture convention for ONE repository; managed policy is for organization-wide rules (compliance, security) and requires central administration. It is heavier than necessary and would apply the rule even in repositories where it makes no sense.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos (a .NET monorepo with 40 projects), the xUnit tests are scattered: in src/*/Tests/, in tests/Integration/, and in folders created for each new service. The root CLAUDE.md already has 400 lines, and half of them are testing conventions (Method_Scenario_Result naming, use of FluentAssertions, builders instead of constructors). What is the best way to organize these conventions?
opcoes: Create .claude/rules/testing.md with paths: (e.g., "**/*Tests.cs", "tests/**") and remove these conventions from the root CLAUDE.md.
Create a CLAUDE.md inside each test folder with the conventions.
Keep everything in the root CLAUDE.md, but move the testing conventions to the end of the file.
Turn the conventions into a "testing-conventions" skill and rely on auto-loading via the description.
questoes.explicacao: Cross-cutting convention (spans directories) → a file in .claude/rules/ with a paths: glob. It loads only when relevant, covers future directories, and avoids duplication.
feedbacks: Correct. A rule with paths: is loaded only when files matching the glob are touched, automatically covers future test folders, and takes weight off the root CLAUDE.md (less context in every session).
Tempting because a subdirectory CLAUDE.md also loads on demand. But it duplicates the same text across dozens of folders, the copies drift, and every new service has to remember to create its own.
Tempting because it is the minimal change. But the file still loads in full in every session (even when nobody touches tests), and the position in the file does not solve the context cost.

Tempting because skills also load on demand. But a skill is for procedures/workflows; loading depends on the model deciding to invoke it. A convention that must always apply whenever a test file is touched is exactly the case for a rule with paths:, which is deterministic via the glob.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, the team wants a /new-migration skill that generates an EF Core migration, runs dotnet ef, and updates the snapshot. Because it has side effects on the development database, it must run ONLY when a dev explicitly calls it, and it must be available to the whole team. Which two decisions meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Put the skill in .claude/skills/new-migration/SKILL.md, versioned in the repository.
Put the skill in each dev's ~/.claude/skills/new-migration/SKILL.md.
Set user-invocable: false in the frontmatter.
Set disable-model-invocation: true in the frontmatter.
Set context: fork in the frontmatter, so that the side effects are isolated in a subagent.
questoes.explicacao: Share with the team → project skill (.claude/skills/). Explicit invocation only → disable-model-invocation: true. user-invocable: false is the opposite; context: fork does not control who invokes it.
feedbacks: Correct. The project's .claude/skills/ is shared via git: all devs get /new-migration.
Tempting because personal skills take precedence over project skills. But they live outside the repository: each dev would have to install it, and the versions drift.
Name trap: user-invocable: false does the opposite of what was asked. It hides the skill from the / menu and lets only the model invoke it.
Correct. It prevents Claude from loading the skill on its own based on the description; it runs only when the dev types /new-migration.

Tempting because "isolate" sounds like safety. But context: fork isolates the CONTEXT (history) in a subagent; the commands still run on the same machine and against the same database, and the skill can still be auto-invoked.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, a squad is going to migrate serialization from Newtonsoft.Json to System.Text.Json. The change affects ~60 files across 9 projects, there are custom converters and known behavioral differences (case sensitivity, dates, ignored fields), and there are two possible strategies (gradual migration with an adapter, or a direct swap). How should the dev carry out this task in Claude Code?
opcoes: Execute directly in acceptEdits mode, asking Claude to migrate everything at once, run the test suite at the end, and fix whatever breaks.
Use plan mode: explore the usages and converters, propose the strategy and the steps, approve the plan, and only then execute.
Use bypassPermissions so that the long migration is not interrupted by permission prompts.
Open 60 separate prompts, one per file, in direct execution, to keep each change small.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode for multi-file, architectural changes with several valid approaches. Direct execution is for fixes with obvious scope.
feedbacks: Tempting because of the speed. But with a large scope and two valid approaches, starting to edit without exploring and agreeing on the strategy causes rework across dozens of files if the choice turns out to be wrong.
Correct. A multi-file change, an architectural decision, and more than one valid approach are exactly the triggers for plan mode: explore and design before editing.
Tempting because the task is long. But bypassPermissions removes the safeguards and is not routine for a long, non-contained task; besides, it does not address the lack of planning.
Tempting because small changes are reviewable. But the changes are interrelated (shared converters and behavior): slicing without a common strategy produces inconsistent decisions across files.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, after an incident, a squad decided to "use plan mode for every single task". Today, a dev got a NullReferenceException with a stack trace pointing to line 87 of FeeService.cs: a check for whether customer.Plan is null is missing before the rate is read. What is the best course of action?
opcoes: Keep plan mode, because the squad's rule exists to prevent incidents.
Invoke the Plan subagent to map all usages of customer.Plan in the monorepo before fixing, so that no other spots are left unhandled.
Create a /fix-null skill with the step-by-step procedure for null fixes, to standardize this kind of fix.
Execute directly: ask for the null check in FeeService.cs, with the stack trace, and review the diff.
questoes.explicacao: Direct execution for a single-file fix with clear scope (null check, constant, bug with a stack trace). Plan mode is a tool for uncertainty and large scope, not a ritual.
feedbacks: Tempting because it follows the rule. But plan mode on a one-line fix with a known cause only adds a round of exploration and approval without reducing any risk.
Tempting because it seems careful. But the bug has a stack trace and a clear cause; mapping the entire repository is exploration out of proportion to the problem.
Tempting because it standardizes. But this is a one-off fix; creating a reusable artifact for a one-line fix is complexity with no payoff.
Correct. Obvious scope, one file, cause explicit in the stack trace: direct execution is the right choice. Reviewing the diff is already sufficient control.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, the project CLAUDE.md states prominently: "NEVER edit files in src/Pomar.Cards/Encryption/ (PCI scope)". Even so, an audit found 2 sessions out of ~80 in which Claude edited these files during broad refactorings. What is the appropriate fix?
opcoes: Rewrite the instruction in capital letters, repeat it at the beginning and end of CLAUDE.md, and add examples of requests that must be refused.
Move the instruction to the managed policy CLAUDE.md, which takes precedence over the project one.
A PreToolUse hook (matcher Edit|Write) in .claude/settings.json that blocks paths in src/Pomar.Cards/Encryption/ with exit 2.
Require mandatory human review by the security team on the PR whenever any file in this folder appears in the diff, blocking the merge until approval.
questoes.explicacao: Security/compliance consequence → programmatic enforcement (PreToolUse hook or deny permission rule). An instruction in CLAUDE.md, however emphatic, is probabilistic.
feedbacks: Tempting because reinforcing the prompt sometimes reduces failures. But a prompt is probabilistic: the failure rate never reaches zero, and a compliance rule (PCI) requires a guarantee.
Tempting because managed policy sounds "official". But it is still a natural-language instruction to the model: it changes who administers the text, not the fact that it is best-effort.
Correct. A critical compliance rule goes into deterministic code: the hook runs before the tool and blocks the edit in 100% of cases, returning the reason to Claude.
Tempting because it is a real control. But it acts after the fact (it detects, it does not prevent) and depends on the reviewer noticing; the requirement is that Claude not edit these files.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, the security team wants a reusable "security reviewer": with its own system prompt focused on OWASP and PCI, READ-ONLY access to the code, and available to all devs in the monorepo, so that the review does not pollute the main session. Which configuration meets these requirements?
opcoes: A custom subagent in .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md, versioned, with a description and tools: Read, Grep, Glob.
An instruction in the project CLAUDE.md: "when asked for a security review, act as an OWASP specialist and do not edit files".
The same subagent, but in ~/.claude/agents/security-reviewer.md on each dev's machine.
Use the built-in general-purpose subagent, passing the OWASP checklist in the prompt of each call.
questoes.explicacao: Custom subagents live in .claude/agents/ (project) with frontmatter (description, tools, model...). Restricting tools in the frontmatter is the real "read-only" control.
feedbacks: Correct. A custom subagent in .claude/agents/ has its own prompt, a restricted tool list (read-only), a context isolated from the main session, and is shared via git.

Tempting because it is simple. But it runs in the main session (it pollutes the context and reviews with the bias of whoever generated the code), and "do not edit" in a prompt does not actually restrict the tools.
Tempting because the definition is identical. But user scope is personal: it does not reach the 40 devs through the repository, and the versions drift.
Tempting because general-purpose already exists. But it has access to the write tools, and the checklist would have to be repeated in every call, with no standardization.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, after 40 minutes discussing the "pre-approved credit limit" rule with Claude (CreditLimitPolicy class, exception for Gold plan customers), the dev asks: "use an Explore subagent to find where that rule we discussed is validated". The subagent comes back with a generic answer about "typical limit validations". What is the cause, and what is the fix?
opcoes: Explore has no access to Grep; the fix is to use the general-purpose subagent.
The subagent does not inherit the history; the delegation prompt must include the rule, the CreditLimitPolicy class, the Gold plan exception, and the return format.
The subagent hit its turn limit before finishing the search; the fix is to increase its maximum number of turns and ask for a more exhaustive search of the monorepo.
The main context was full; the fix is to run /compact before delegating.
questoes.explicacao: A subagent's context is isolated: it does not see the parent's history. Delegate with a self-contained prompt (what, where, criteria, return format).
feedbacks: Tempting because switching subagents seems to solve it. But Explore has Grep, Glob, and Read; changing the type does not change the problem: general-purpose also starts without the history.
Correct. A fresh subagent has an isolated context: "that rule we discussed" means nothing to it. Everything it needs goes explicitly in the prompt.
Tempting because an incomplete answer looks like a cutoff caused by a limit. But the answer was not cut off, it was generic: what is missing is information, not time.
Tempting because the session was long. But /compact affects the main session's context, not the subagent's, which still receives only the delegation prompt.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, before replacing the currency enum with ISO 4217 codes, the dev asks Claude for an impact analysis of three independent modules: Billing, Reconciliation, and Reports. Currently Claude delegates to a subagent, waits for the result, delegates the next one, and the process takes 25 minutes. How can the time be reduced without losing quality?
opcoes: Delegate the three modules to a single subagent, which analyzes them in sequence within its own context.
Let the three subagents exchange findings directly with each other to avoid duplicate work.
Open three terminals with independent Claude Code sessions, one per module, and manually paste the three results into the main session for consolidation.
Ask Claude to launch the three subagents in the same response (multiple Agent calls), with defined scopes, and consolidate.
questoes.explicacao: Subagent parallelism = multiple Agent calls in the same response. Separate turns = sequential. Communication always goes through the coordinator.
feedbacks: Tempting because it reduces the number of delegations. But it is still sequential, and it concentrates three noisy analyses in a single context, which worsens the quality of the report.
Tempting because it seems efficient. But subagents do not talk to each other; communication goes through the coordinator (hub-and-spoke), which aggregates and deduplicates.
Tempting because it does parallelize. But it is manual, loses the aggregation done by the coordinator, and does not take advantage of Claude Code's native parallelism feature.
Correct. Multiple Agent calls in the same response run in parallel; delegations in separate turns are sequential. The coordinator consolidates the three results.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, yesterday a dev worked in the session named "refactor-fees". Overnight, a colleague merged a PR that renamed half of the classes the session had read and edited. Today the dev wants to continue the work. Which two practices are appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Start a new session, providing a structured summary of yesterday's decisions and of what remains to be done.
Resume with claude --resume refactor-fees and continue where it left off, with no additional comments.
Resume with --fork-session, because the fork creates a new session that automatically reloads the files changed since the original session.
Increase the turn limit of the resumed session so that Claude has time to rediscover the changes.
If resuming, explicitly state what changed (merged PR, renamed classes) and ask it to reread the affected files.
questoes.explicacao: --resume is good when the tool results are still valid. If the code changed: a new session with a structured summary, or resume while explicitly stating what changed. --fork-session does not refresh anything.
feedbacks: Correct. With changed files, the tool results in the history are stale; a new session with a structured summary starts from the actual state of the code.
Tempting because it preserves all the reasoning. But the history contains reads of files that have changed: Claude will act on names and contents that no longer exist.
Trap: --fork-session only creates a new session ID from the same base, so that the branches do not contaminate each other. The copied history still contains the stale results.
Tempting because more turns give more leeway. But the problem is not a lack of turns; it is stale information in the context that Claude does not know is stale.
Correct. When resuming after changes, say explicitly what changed: that way Claude knows which results in the history are no longer valid.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, Claude needs to find all implementations of the IFeeCalculator interface in the monorepo (~2,000 .cs files). The class names do not follow a pattern (e.g., PixFee, BoletoCalculation, CreditCardFee). What is the most efficient approach with the built-in tools?
opcoes: Grep for the content (": IFeeCalculator", ", IFeeCalculator") and Read only the files found.
Use Glob with the pattern "**/*FeeCalculator*.cs" and read the returned files.
Read every file in the Domain folder and in the payment projects, to make sure no implementation slips through.
Ask Claude to list the implementations based on what it "knows" about the project from CLAUDE.md.
questoes.explicacao: Grep = content; Glob = file names/paths. To find who implements an interface, search by content and read only the hits.
feedbacks: Correct. Grep searches inside file contents, so it finds the implementation declaration whatever the class name; Read is then limited to the hits.
Tempting because Glob is fast. But Glob matches file NAMES; since the classes have varied names, several implementations would be left out.
Tempting because of the completeness. But reading everything up front is the exploration anti-pattern: it consumes context with hundreds of irrelevant files.
Tempting because CLAUDE.md describes the architecture. But it is not a class index; the answer would be a guess instead of a search of the code.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, Claude tries to replace a "return null;" with "return Result.Failure(Errors.CustomerNotFound);" in CustomerRepository.cs, but the Edit tool fails: the old_string snippet appears 6 times in the file. Only one of the occurrences should change. What is the correct action?
opcoes: Repeat the Edit with replace_all: true to make sure the replacement happens.
Expand old_string with neighboring lines until the snippet is unique, and repeat the Edit.
Rewrite the whole file with Write from what Claude remembers of its content, without rereading it.
Use Bash with sed to replace the first occurrence of "return null;".
questoes.explicacao: Edit fails when the snippet is not unique: expand the snippet (or read the whole file and rewrite it). replace_all changes every occurrence.
feedbacks: Tempting because it makes the Edit go through. But it replaces all 6 occurrences, and only one should change; the uniqueness error was protecting against exactly that.
Correct. Edit requires a unique snippet; including the surrounding context identifies the right occurrence without touching the others.
Tempting because it works around Edit. But rewriting from memory risks deleting or altering code; if the file is going to be rewritten, it must be read in full first.
Tempting because sed is fast. But "the first occurrence" may not be the right one; it is a positional guess, without the uniqueness guarantee.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, Claude generates entity-to-DTO mappers, but gets the team's conventions wrong (Response suffix instead of Dto, dates as DateTimeOffset in UTC, monetary amounts in cents as long). Two attempts with prose instructions in the prompt did not solve it. Which two actions tend to be the most effective? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Repeat the instructions in capital letters, with "IMPORTANT" at the beginning and end of the prompt, listing each convention on a separate line.
Show 2 or 3 concrete pairs that already exist in the repository (entity → correct DTO), highlighting what each one demonstrates.
Increase effort to max, so that Claude reasons more about the conventions.
First write failing tests that describe the mapper's expected output, and ask Claude to iterate until they pass.
Ask Claude to "pay more attention to the team's conventions" and to review its own output before answering.
questoes.explicacao: Iterative refinement: concrete examples (2–3 pairs) and failing tests beat prose instructions. Emphasis, effort, and "pay attention" provide no new information.
feedbacks: Tempting because emphasis sometimes helps. But the prose has already failed twice; the problem is a lack of concreteness, not of volume.
Correct. Concrete input/output examples communicate conventions more precisely than prose and teach the pattern so that it generalizes.
Tempting because more reasoning seems to help. But Claude is not getting it wrong for lack of effort: it does not have a concrete reference for the convention.
Correct. TDD turns the convention into a verifiable criterion: Claude receives the specific failures and iterates until it complies.
Tempting because it is simple. But it is a vague criterion, and self-review in the same session inherits the same misunderstanding that produced the output.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, the /review-pr skill instructs: "point out only the important issues". The devs complain that the same change gets 0 comments one day and 12 the next, mixing security flaws with style preferences. What is the best improvement?
opcoes: Change it to "be rigorous and point out all issues", leaving the filtering to the dev.
Limit the output to at most 5 comments per PR, ordered by the importance perceived by the model, so that the dev reads only what matters most and the volume stays stable.
Add a second call to a model to filter the comments from the first one.
Explicit criteria: what counts (e.g., concatenated SQL, money as double), what does not count (analyzer-covered style), and boundary examples.
questoes.explicacao: "Use your good judgment"/"only the important ones" lead to inconsistency. For each judgment call: what counts, what does not count, and boundary examples.
feedbacks: Tempting because it eliminates the problem of missed findings. But it swaps one vague criterion for another ("rigorous") and increases noise, which erodes trust in the comments.
Tempting because it controls the volume. But an arbitrary cutoff does not define what is important; it remains inconsistent and may cut the security flaw.
Tempting because it sounds robust. But it is more complex and inherits the same vague criterion; the simplest fix is to define the criterion.
Correct. Explicit criteria, with what counts, what does not count, and boundary examples, make the judgment reproducible. It is the simplest fix that solves the problem.

questoes.pergunta: At Pomar Pagamentos, after 4 hours in the same refactoring session on the Reconciliation module, Claude starts suggesting "typical reconciliation patterns" instead of citing the project's classes, and forgets decisions made at the beginning (e.g., the name of the new aggregate and the 0.01 rounding tolerance). What is the best course of action?
opcoes: Save decisions and state to a progress file, run /compact (or start a new session) from it, and delegate explorations to subagents.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so that the entire session fits.
Disable automatic compaction so that nothing from the beginning of the session is lost.
Manually repeat, in each new prompt, the list of decisions made so far.
questoes.explicacao: Degraded context in a long session: state in a file (scratchpad), proactive /compact or a new session with a summary, and subagents for exploration.
feedbacks: Correct. Generic answers and forgotten decisions are signs of context degradation. A scratchpad file survives compression, a proactive /compact clears the noise, and subagents keep exploration out of the main context.
Tempting because a larger window seems to solve it. But a large window is expensive (every token on every turn) and "lost in the middle" gets worse; it does not address the accumulated noise.
Tempting because the loss came over time. But the degradation comes from excess context, not just from compaction; disabling it leads to overflowing the window.
Tempting because it works in the short term. But it is fragile and manual, and it adds even more text to an already saturated session. A state file does the same thing persistently.

questoes.pergunta:
SCENARIO — The State Court of Audit of Serra Azul (TCE Serra Azul, a fictional agency) maintains the system that receives and analyzes the financial accountability reports of 300 municipalities: 1.8 million lines spread across a legacy Java 8 core (built with Ant), new C# services, and hundreds of SQL scripts. The IT department is about to receive 12 analyst-developers hired through the civil-service exam and wants to use Claude Code to speed up onboarding and maintenance, with MCP servers for Redmine (tickets), a read-only PostgreSQL replica, and the technical wiki. Constraints: personal data of civil servants is confidential; credentials never go into git; and much of the system's knowledge is undocumented.

Problem: a new analyst asks Claude: "how is the penalty for late submission of the accountability report calculated?". Which exploration strategy should Claude follow?
opcoes: Read all the files in the oversight module up front to have the complete picture before answering.
First generate an index of all classes and tables in the repository in CLAUDE.md, and then answer the question from that index.
Grep for the entry points ("penalty", "late", the endpoint), read those files, and follow the relevant dependencies with Grep.
Use WebSearch to find out how audit courts usually calculate penalties and explain based on that.
questoes.explicacao: Incremental exploration: grep for entry points → read → follow imports with grep → read. Reading everything up front wastes context.
feedbacks: Tempting because of the completeness. But reading everything up front is the exploration anti-pattern: the module has hundreds of files, and the context fills up with irrelevant code.
Tempting because it seems like a useful investment. But it is out of proportion to the question, bloats the CLAUDE.md that loads in every session, and goes stale with every commit.
Correct. Grep for the entry points, read, and Grep again following the dependencies: understanding is built up gradually, with context spent only on what matters.
Tempting because the code is undocumented. But the question is about THIS system; the rule found on the web may differ from what is implemented.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, an analyst is investigating which routines write to the TB_CASE table. The searches produce thousands of lines of Grep output (Java, C#, and SQL), and after a few rounds Claude in the main session starts to lose track of the original task. What is the best way to conduct this investigation?
opcoes: Increase MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS so that no output gets truncated.
Delegate the investigation to an Explore subagent with a defined goal and return format, receiving only the conclusion.
Run /clear between one search and the next to keep the context clean, manually noting what was found in each round before clearing.
Replace Grep with Glob in all searches, because Glob returns fewer lines.
questoes.explicacao: Voluminous exploration → an Explore subagent that returns only the conclusion. It keeps the main context clean.
feedbacks: Tempting because it deals with an output limit. But that variable applies to the output of MCP tools, and the problem here is the opposite: too much output entering the main context.
Correct. A voluminous, noisy search is work for a subagent: the noise stays in its context, and the main session receives only the summary.
Tempting because it cleans the context. But /clear also wipes out the goal and the previous findings; the investigation starts from scratch every round.
Tempting because it reduces the output. But Glob matches file names, not content: it does not find who writes to the table.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, the Redmine MCP server (remote, HTTP) must be available to all analysts who clone the system's repository, but each one authenticates with their own personal token. Which configuration is correct?
opcoes: Run claude mcp add with the default scope on each machine, pasting the token into the command.
Declare the server in .claude/settings.local.json, since each analyst has their own token.
Declare the server in .mcp.json at the root with the literal token of a service account, so that nobody needs to configure anything.
Declare it in .mcp.json (project scope) with type "http", the url, and an authorization header using ${REDMINE_TOKEN}.
questoes.explicacao: Share with the team → .mcp.json (project). Secrets via ${VAR}, never literals. The MCP local scope ≠ settings.local.json.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is the quickest path. But the default scope is local: it applies only to that user in that project, is stored in ~/.claude.json, and is not shared through the repository.
Name trap: the MCP "local" scope is not settings.local.json. That file is personal and gitignored, and it is not where servers are declared for the team.
Tempting because it is convenient. But it puts a literal secret in a versioned file and erases per-user traceability.
Correct. Project scope (.mcp.json) is shared via git; ${VAR} expansion keeps the secret out of the file, and each analyst uses their own credential.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, an analyst added the technical wiki to .mcp.json like this: {"mcpServers": {"wiki": {"url": "https://wiki.tce-sa.gov.br/mcp"}}}. The server does not start, and Claude does not see any wiki tools. The endpoint works with Streamable HTTP. What is the fix?
opcoes: Add "type": "http" to the server entry.
Change the url to the wiki's SSE endpoint, which is the default transport for remote servers.
Wrap the URL in a small local stdio proxy declared with command and args.
Add headers with an authentication token, because the server rejects anonymous connections.
questoes.explicacao: Classic trap: a url without a type is read as stdio and fails. A remote server always declares its type ("http" for Streamable HTTP).
feedbacks: Correct. Without type, the entry is treated as a stdio server (local, launched via command) and fails; a remote server must declare its transport. Streamable HTTP is "http".
Tempting because SSE is remote. But SSE is the legacy transport; and the problem is not the chosen transport, it is the missing type.
Tempting because it works around the failure. But it creates an extra component to solve what a single property solves; unnecessary complexity.
Tempting because a connection failure looks like an authentication problem. But the entry is not even treated as remote; without type, headers make no difference.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, two MCP servers expose search tools: the wiki has search ("searches stuff") and Redmine has find ("looks things up in the system"). When the analyst asks for the ticket for a bug, Claude often queries the wiki, and vice versa. Which two actions address the cause? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Rewrite the descriptions: what each tool covers, when to use it, an example input, and how it differs from the other.
Put a classifier in front of Claude that decides, based on keywords, which server to send the question to.
Rename the tools to names that reveal their purpose, such as wiki_search_pages and redmine_search_tickets.
Add to CLAUDE.md: "for tickets use find; for documentation use search".
Disable the wiki server until the problem has been investigated.
questoes.explicacao: Overlapping tools with vague descriptions → wrong routing. Fix it at the source: names and descriptions that say when to use each tool and how they differ. A classifier is premature complexity.
feedbacks: Correct. The description is the tool selection criterion. Vague, overlapping descriptions cause the wrong routing; differentiating them explicitly addresses the cause.
Tempting because it is deterministic. But it is more complex than necessary: the simplest fix (better descriptions and names) comes before a routing component.
Correct. The name also guides selection; generic, similar names (search/find) reinforce the confusion.
Tempting because it is quick. But it patches the symptom outside the tool: the tool definition remains ambiguous for any other client or context in which that CLAUDE.md is not present.
Tempting because it eliminates the routing error. But it also eliminates the ability to query the documentation; it trades a selection problem for a loss of functionality.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, IT wants Claude Code, for all analysts, to be able to run git log, git diff, and git status without asking for permission, but never to execute git push or rm -rf. The rule must apply to the whole team and be reviewable. Where and how should this be configured?
opcoes: In the project CLAUDE.md: "you may use git log/diff/status freely; never run git push or rm -rf".
In .claude/settings.json (versioned), with permissions.allow for git log/diff/status (e.g., Bash(git log *)) and permissions.deny for Bash(git push *) and Bash(rm -rf *).
In each analyst's .claude/settings.local.json, with the same allow/deny rules.
Start every session with --dangerously-skip-permissions, to eliminate permission prompts, and rely on a CLAUDE.md instruction to avoid git push and rm -rf.
questoes.explicacao: Team permissions → .claude/settings.json (project, versioned) with allow/deny. Local settings are personal; CLAUDE.md enforces nothing.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is readable by everyone. But an instruction in CLAUDE.md is probabilistic: it neither pre-approves anything nor actually blocks a command.
Correct. Permission rules in the project settings are shared via git and enforced by the harness, not by the model: allow pre-approves, deny blocks.
Tempting because the rules are right. But settings.local.json is personal and gitignored: it is neither shared with nor reviewable by the team.
Tempting because it eliminates permission prompts. But it removes all safeguards and leaves the protection against push and rm -rf only in the prompt; it is the opposite of what was asked.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, the Java core lives in legacy/ and has its own conventions (built with Ant, Java 8 without lambdas as required by the application server, ISO-8859-1 encoding). These instructions only matter when someone touches that folder; today they are in the root CLAUDE.md and take up context in every session, including the C# ones. What is the best organization?
opcoes: Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md, but inside a section titled "legacy/ only".
Move them to docs/legacy.md and import it into the root CLAUDE.md with @docs/legacy.md, leaving the root leaner.
Move them to the personal CLAUDE.md of whoever works on the legacy code.
Move them to legacy/CLAUDE.md, loaded on demand when files in legacy/ are read.
questoes.explicacao: Instructions that apply to one directory → that subdirectory's CLAUDE.md (loads on demand). @imports and sections in the root always load.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is minimal. But a heading changes nothing about loading: the text still enters every session.
Tempting because it organizes the file. But an @import is expanded when the importing file loads; since the root always loads, so does the imported content.
Tempting because only a few devs touch the legacy code. But this is system knowledge, not a personal preference: any analyst who touches the folder needs it.
Correct. A subdirectory CLAUDE.md enters the context when Claude reads files in that folder. It is specific, versioned, and adds no weight to sessions that do not touch the legacy code.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, the senior analysts wrote a 9-step procedure for producing the "change impact report" required by the committee (identify affected tables, look up related tickets in Redmine, build the risk matrix, etc.). It is used a few times a month. Where should this procedure live?
opcoes: In a project skill (.claude/skills/change-impact-report/SKILL.md) with a description saying when to use it.
In the root CLAUDE.md, so that Claude always knows how to build the report.
In a UserPromptSubmit hook that injects the procedure whenever the prompt contains the word "impact".
In a .claude/rules/impact.md file without frontmatter.
questoes.explicacao: Occasional procedure/workflow → skill (loads on demand; /command). CLAUDE.md and rules without paths always load.
feedbacks: Correct. A reusable, occasional procedure is the typical case for a skill: the body only enters the context when it is used, and the whole team gets it via git.
Tempting because it guarantees availability. But the 9 steps would take up context in every session for something used a few times a month.
Tempting because it is automatic. But it reinvents, with fragile code (a keyword), what the skill already does, and it fires on prompts that merely mention "impact" in passing.
Tempting because rules organize instructions. But a rule without paths: loads at the start of every session, at the same cost as leaving it in CLAUDE.md.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, the PostgreSQL replica is exposed via MCP (tool mcp__pg__query). Some tables contain civil servants' CPFs (Brazilian taxpayer IDs), and the confidentiality policy requires that CPFs never enter the model's context or the transcripts. Queries against these tables, however, are legitimate for debugging calculation rules. Which control meets the requirement?
opcoes: An instruction in CLAUDE.md: "never display CPFs in your answers".
A PreToolUse hook that blocks any query mentioning the tables that contain CPFs, returning guidance to Claude to query another source.
A PostToolUse hook (matcher mcp__pg__.*) that masks the CPFs in the result before it reaches the model.
A Stop hook that examines the final answer and deletes CPFs before showing it to the analyst.
questoes.explicacao: PostToolUse = normalize/clean/mask results (e.g., PII) before they reach the model. PreToolUse blocks the call; Stop acts only at the end.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is simple. But the CPF would already have entered the context by arriving in the tool result; the prompt only tries not to repeat it, and even that is probabilistic.
Tempting because it is deterministic. But it blocks legitimate debugging queries; the requirement is to hide the CPF, not to forbid the tables.
Correct. PostToolUse runs after the tool and before the model sees the result: it is the point at which to normalize and mask PII deterministically, without preventing the query.
Tempting because it is a filter in code. But it acts too late: the CPF has already passed through the context and the transcript.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, an analyst wrote a PreToolUse hook (type command, matcher Bash) that detects psql commands containing DELETE, UPDATE, or DROP and terminates with exit 1 and a message on stderr. In testing, the message appears, but the commands still execute. What is the cause?
opcoes: PreToolUse hooks only intercept MCP tools; for Bash commands you need a PostToolUse hook, which sees the fully assembled command.
Exit 1 is a non-blocking error; to block, the hook must exit with exit 2 (or return permissionDecision deny).
The matcher must be "Bash(psql*)" for the hook to intercept psql commands.
Project hooks cannot block commands; only managed policy hooks have that power.
questoes.explicacao: Command hook: exit 0 = proceed; exit 2 = block (stderr goes back to Claude); other codes = non-blocking error. Alternative: JSON with permissionDecision deny.
feedbacks: Tempting because there are different hooks for different moments. But PreToolUse applies to any tool, including Bash; and PostToolUse would run after the command, too late to block it.
Correct. In command hooks, exit 0 proceeds and exit 2 blocks (stderr becomes feedback for Claude). Other codes are non-blocking errors: the tool runs anyway.
Tempting because it resembles the syntax of permission rules. But the hook is already being triggered (the message appears); the problem is the exit code.
Tempting because managed policy sounds stronger. But project hooks block normally; where the configuration lives does not change the semantics of the exit code.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, management asks Claude to "document the procurement module", which nobody on the current team knows. It is not known how many subsystems exist, what integrations there are with other modules, or where the rules live. Which decomposition strategy is most appropriate?
opcoes: Prompt chaining with fixed steps defined in advance: 1) list classes, 2) list tables, 3) list endpoints, 4) consolidate and write the final module document.
A single prompt asking for the complete document, so that Claude has the full picture.
Split the work in advance by directory, with one subagent per folder, each one documenting its own.
Dynamic decomposition: map the structure and integrations first, generate the subtasks from what was discovered, and do another round for the gaps.
questoes.explicacao: Steps known in advance → prompt chaining. Open-ended investigation → dynamic/adaptive decomposition, with an extra round for the gaps.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is predictable. But prompt chaining is for when the steps are known in advance; here, the structure of the module is precisely what needs to be discovered.
Tempting because it is simple. But a large, open-ended investigation in a single step leads to shallow coverage and undetected gaps.
Tempting because it parallelizes. But splitting by folder is arbitrary: the rules and integrations cut across directories, and a fixed decomposition ignores what the exploration will reveal.
Correct. In an open-ended investigation, the subtasks emerge from the findings: map, decompose based on the map, and do a targeted round for whatever is still missing.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, the analyst asks Claude to find out who reads and writes the TB_CASE table in three independent codebases: the Java core, the C# services, and the scheduled SQL scripts. Claude is going to use Explore subagents. Which two orchestration practices are the most appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Have the three subagents exchange results directly with each other to eliminate duplicates before answering.
Launch the three subagents in the same coordinator response, so that they run in parallel.
Use a single subagent for the three codebases, so that it has a shared view.
Paste the full transcript of the 3-hour session into each subagent's prompt, since subagents do not inherit the history and need all the context.
Give each subagent a self-contained prompt: table, codebase, what counts as a read/write, and return format (file, line, operation).
questoes.explicacao: Independent subagents in parallel (same response) + a self-contained prompt with scope and format. Communication goes through the coordinator; no dumping of the transcript.
feedbacks: Tempting because deduplicating early seems efficient. But subagents do not communicate directly; the coordinator receives the results and consolidates them (hub-and-spoke).
Correct. The three codebases are independent; multiple Agent calls in the same response run in parallel.
Tempting because of the integrated view. But it serializes the work and concentrates three noisy searches in a single context; integration is the coordinator's role.
Tempting because the subagent does not inherit the history. But it dumps noise; the right approach is to pass only what the task requires, in a structured way.
Correct. The subagent's context is isolated; a self-contained prompt, with scope and return format, allows the coordinator to aggregate the three results.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, Claude classifies legacy code snippets as "high", "medium", or "low" risk to prioritize modernization. The written rule is clear for the extremes, but the analysts often disagree with the classifications in boundary cases (e.g., dynamic SQL with parameters coming only from an internal enum). What is the best improvement?
opcoes: Include 3 or 4 examples of boundary cases, each with the snippet, the classification, and the reasoning.
Include 20 examples of obvious high- and low-risk cases to reinforce the rule.
Ask Claude to assign a confidence score to each classification and send cases below 0.7 to human review.
Add "use your good judgment in ambiguous cases".
questoes.explicacao: Ambiguous cases → 2–4 examples targeted at the boundary, with input, output, and reasoning. Good judgment and self-reported confidence do not solve it.
feedbacks: Correct. Few-shot examples targeted at the ambiguous cases, with explicit reasoning, teach the tie-breaking criterion. This is the classic use of examples.
Tempting because more examples seem better. But the extremes already work; obvious examples do not teach the boundary, and the volume can lead to memorizing instead of generalizing.
Tempting because it uses human review. But self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and this does not improve the criterion; it only shifts the doubt elsewhere.
Tempting because it sounds flexible. But it is exactly the vague criterion that causes inconsistency.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, during a long investigation session, Claude gathered exact figures: tickets #48213 and #48977, the TB_CASE_HIST_2019 table, and the resolution's 180-day limit. After a /compact, it started citing "a ticket from 2019" and "about six months". What is the best practice for future investigations?
opcoes: Avoid /compact and let the session grow up to the window limit.
Ask Claude, after the /compact, to remember the exact figures cited earlier.
Keep a notes file with the case facts (IDs, tables, deadlines, exact values), updated as they come up.
Use a model with a larger window so that /compact is never necessary.
questoes.explicacao: Summaries lose exact values, IDs, and dates. Keep "case facts" in a persistent file/block that is never summarized.
feedbacks: Tempting because the loss came from the summary. But the session degrades with excess context and ends up overflowing the window; postponing compression does not protect the data.
Tempting because it is quick. But the detail has already been summarized away and lost; asking it to "remember" invites it to invent plausible values.
Correct. Summaries lose exact values, IDs, and dates. A persistent block of case facts, outside the summarized history, preserves what cannot be paraphrased.
Tempting because it postpones the problem. But a larger window is expensive and suffers from "lost in the middle"; the risk of losing exact facts remains.

questoes.pergunta: At TCE Serra Azul, on a Monday, an analyst asked: "are there open tickets about the penalty calculation?". Claude answered "there are no open tickets on this topic". It later turned out that the VPN was down and that the Redmine MCP server, upon failing to connect, returned an empty list. What is the appropriate fix?
opcoes: Instruct Claude, in CLAUDE.md, to distrust empty lists coming from Redmine and to always run the search twice before concluding that there are no tickets.
Configure the server to respond "Operation failed" when the connection drops.
Add a Stop hook that blocks answers containing "there are no tickets".
On a connection failure, the server returns a structured error (isError, transient, retryable); an empty list only for a query that ran with no results.
questoes.explicacao: Silently suppressing an error (empty as success) is an anti-pattern. Structured error with category and retryability; empty only when the query actually ran.
feedbacks: Tempting because it reduces false "nothing found" answers. But it does not distinguish the situations: if the search fails twice, the empty list still looks like success.
Tempting because at least it signals failure. But it is the generic-error anti-pattern: it does not say what failed, whether it is transient, or what to do.
Tempting because it is deterministic. But it would also block correct "nothing found" answers; the defect is at the source of the signal, not in the phrase.

Correct. Empty is not failure: an empty list returned successfully is information; a timeout or a dropped connection means the search did not run. The structured error lets Claude retry or alert the analyst.

questoes.pergunta:
SCENARIO — Rota Viva Logística runs last-mile delivery routing in 40 cities. Its monorepo has 22 .NET microservices, an Angular app for drivers, and about 300 PRs per week on GitHub Actions. Engineering is bringing Claude Code into the pipeline for three uses: automated PR review (the comments are posted by a bot that parses JSON), test generation for uncovered code, and a nightly technical debt report across 80 repositories. Constraints: no job may hang the pipeline; the monthly cost has a cap; and the devs already ignore tools that generate too many false positives.

Problem: the first review job was written as claude "review this PR's diff and point out issues". It sits idle until it hits the runner's 60-minute timeout, without producing any output. What is the fix?
opcoes: Add --max-turns 5 to limit the execution.
Run in non-interactive mode with -p (--print).
Add --output-format json so that the output comes out structured.
Add --permission-mode bypassPermissions so that no permission prompt blocks the job.
questoes.explicacao: In CI, -p/--print is mandatory: non-interactive execution that prints and exits. The other CI flags (--output-format, --max-turns, --json-schema...) complement -p.
feedbacks: Tempting because it limits the duration. But without -p, Claude Code opens an interactive session and waits for input; the turn limit does not change the execution mode.
Correct. -p runs the prompt, prints the result, and exits. Without it, the process opens an interactive session and waits for input that will never arrive on the runner.
Tempting because the bot needs JSON. But --output-format applies to print mode; without -p, the session remains interactive and stuck.
Tempting because permission prompts can hang the job. But the cause is the interactive session; besides, bypassPermissions removes safeguards unnecessarily.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the review job already runs with -p, but the bot that posts the comments breaks in ~5% of runs: sometimes the response comes with text before the JSON, sometimes inside a markdown block, sometimes without the severity field. What is the most robust fix?
opcoes: Add --append-system-prompt "respond ONLY with valid JSON, no markdown".
Post-process the output with a regex to extract the first block between curly braces.
Switch to --output-format stream-json so that each event comes as JSON.
Use --output-format json with --json-schema and have the bot read the structured_output field.
questoes.explicacao: Machine-consumed output in CI → --output-format json + --json-schema (result in structured_output). Prompt instructions and regex are fragile.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is the obvious instruction. But it is still a prompt: it reduces the failure without eliminating it, and it does not guarantee the required fields.
Tempting because it works around the extra text. But it does not solve a missing field or a wrong type, and it is fragile with nested JSON.
Tempting because of the name. But stream-json is the transport format (events as JSON lines); the content of the response is still free text, with no schema.
Correct. --json-schema makes Claude Code return output validated against the schema, in the structured_output field of the JSON. This addresses format, fields, and types all at once.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the test generation job runs with -p and must be able to read code, create and edit test files, and run dotnet test without being blocked by permission prompts. It must not have web access. Which two configurations meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: --dangerously-skip-permissions, so that no permission prompt blocks the job at any step.
An instruction in CLAUDE.md: "in this job, do not access the internet".
--allowedTools "Read,Edit,Write,Bash(dotnet test *)", pre-approving these tools.
--max-turns 1, so that the job has no turns left over to access the web.
--disallowedTools "WebFetch,WebSearch", which removes these tools from Claude's context.
questoes.explicacao: In CI, define the perimeter with flags: --allowedTools approves what is needed (with scope, such as Bash(dotnet test *)), --disallowedTools removes what should not exist. A prompt is not access control.
feedbacks: Tempting because it eliminates any blocking. But it unlocks everything (including commands and network access the job should not use); it is the opposite of restricting the scope.
Tempting because it is simple. But it is probabilistic; restricting a capability is done by removing the tool, not by asking the model.
Correct. --allowedTools approves the listed tools; with the Bash(dotnet test *) rule, only that command runs without asking for permission.
Tempting because it limits execution. But one turn is not enough to read, write tests, and run them; and it does not remove the ability to access the web.
Correct. A tool name without a scope in --disallowedTools removes the tool entirely: Claude does not even see it, so it cannot use it.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, a "self-correction" job does the following in a single -p invocation: it fixes the failing test and then "critically reviews its own fix". The review almost always approves, and two bugs introduced by the fix reached production. Which architectural change solves this best?
opcoes: Review in a separate invocation (a new session), which receives the diff and the goal, without the generation's reasoning.
Increase the effort of the same invocation so that the self-review is more careful.
Resume the fix session with --resume in a second pipeline step and request the review there, with all the context of what was changed.
Add to the prompt: "be extremely critical, assume there are bugs".
questoes.explicacao: Self-review in the same session is an anti-pattern (context bias). Review in a new session, without the generation's reasoning.
feedbacks: Correct. Reasoning-context bias: whoever generated the fix tends to confirm their own decisions. An independent session reviews the diff without inheriting the justifications.
Tempting because more reasoning seems like more rigor. But the problem is not effort: it is the same context reviewing its own decisions.
Tempting because it splits the work into two steps. But --resume loads the entire generation history; the bias stays the same.
Tempting because it flips the stance. But it is a prompt instruction against a structural bias, and it tends to produce false positives instead of finding the real bugs.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, a refactoring PR touches 45 files across 6 services. The single-pass automated review missed a contract break (a DTO field changed in one service and the consumer in another was not updated) and applied different criteria to similar files. Which review approach is most appropriate?
opcoes: Use a model with a larger window so that the 45 files fit comfortably in a single pass.
Split the PR into batches of 10 files and review each batch in isolation, with the same prompt, posting each batch's findings to the PR as they come out.
Pass 1: review each file locally with the same prompt; pass 2: an integration review that receives the findings and analyzes the contracts between files.
Run the same single-pass review three times and keep only the findings that appear in at least two runs.
questoes.explicacao: Large PR → pass 1 per file (consistency) + pass 2 for integration using the findings (cross-file).
feedbacks: Tempting because the problem seems to be about space. But the problem is diluted attention; fitting in the window guarantees neither consistent analysis nor integration across files.
Tempting because it reduces the load per call. But without an integration pass, the contract break between services remains invisible, because the two sides fall into different batches.
Correct. Multi-pass review: the per-file pass provides consistency and focus; the integration pass catches cross-file bugs (contracts, data flow, errors at the boundary).
Tempting because voting reduces noise. But it repeats the same structural flaw three times; the cross-file bug that a single pass does not see remains unseen.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, there are two candidate flows for the Message Batches API (50% cheaper, results within up to 24h): (1) PR review, which is currently a required check before merge; (2) the nightly technical debt report for the 80 repositories, consumed at the 10 a.m. meeting the following day. What is the correct decision?
opcoes: Move both to batch and cut the cost in half.
Move PR review to batch and have the merge check poll the status every minute until the result comes out.
Keep both synchronous, because batch does not support structured output schemas.
Move only the nightly report to batch and keep PR review synchronous.
questoes.explicacao: Batch: nightly analysis, reports, bulk processing. Never for pre-merge checks, real time, or a blocking CI step.
feedbacks: Tempting because of the savings. But batch has no SLA and can take up to 24h: it would hold up merges on a blocking check.
Tempting because polling seems to work around the wait. But there is no time guarantee; the PR could be blocked for hours.

Tempting because it looks like a technical limitation. But the relevant restrictions of batch are the lack of an SLA and of a multi-turn tool loop within a request; that is no reason to give up the savings on the report.
Correct. Nightly, non-blocking, latency-tolerant work is the ideal case for batch. A pre-merge check and any blocking step need a synchronous response.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the nightly report sends one request per repository in a batch. The script matches results to repositories by position (the 1st result to the 1st repository sent, and so on). The report has been attributing findings from one repository to another. What is the fix?
opcoes: Sort the results by completion time before matching them.
Use a custom_id with the repository identifier and match each result by it.
Send one batch per repository, so that each batch has a single result.
Ask the model to repeat the repository name on the first line of the response and parse it.
questoes.explicacao: Batch results arrive out of order → always match by custom_id.
feedbacks: Tempting because it tries to reconstruct the order. But completion time has no relation to submission order; the matching would still be wrong.
Correct. The results of a batch may come back out of order; custom_id is the correlation key between request and result.
Tempting because it eliminates the ambiguity. But it creates 80 batches to manage and poll, when a single field solves the problem.
Tempting because it works most of the time. But it depends on the model repeating the name correctly; correlation should come from the protocol (custom_id), not from generated text.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the nightly batch of 1,200 requests finished with 1,158 succeeded, 37 errored, and 5 expired. Which two practices are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Resubmit the entire batch with all 1,200 requests, to ensure the report comes from a single, consistent run that is comparable with previous nights.
Treat the 5 expired requests as successes with an empty result, since there was no explicit error.
Resubmit in a new batch only the custom_ids with an errored or expired result (fixing the cause of the errors first, if it is a validation issue).
Increase the batch expiration time to 72h, so that no request expires.
Read the results only after processing_status reaches "ended", and then handle each result according to its type (succeeded, errored, canceled, expired).
questoes.explicacao: Batch: poll until processing_status = ended, then handle each result by type. Resubmit only the custom_ids that failed; never treat expired as an empty success.
feedbacks: Tempting because of the consistency. But it pays again for 1,158 valid results; resubmit only what failed.
Tempting because expired is not errored. But expired means the request was not processed within the window; treating it as empty is silently suppressing a failure.
Correct. Resubmit only the custom_ids that failed; if the error lies in the request itself (validation), fix it before resubmitting.
Tempting because it addresses the cause of the expirations. But the batch processing window is up to 24h; there is no way to extend it to 72h.
Correct. Poll until ended; then each individual result reports the outcome of its request.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the automated review has a "possible null reference" category that fires on almost every PR, and 80% of those findings are dismissed. The devs have started ignoring ALL of the bot's comments, including the security ones, which are usually right. What is the best immediate action?
opcoes: Turn off the noisy category, rewrite its criterion (what counts, what does not, examples), and turn it back on after measuring its precision.
Ask Claude for a confidence score per finding and post only those above 0.8.
Add to the prompt: "be conservative when flagging null references".
Add a second model that filters the first one's comments before posting, discarding the ones it judges to be false positives.
questoes.explicacao: A noisy category contaminates trust in all of them: turn it off, define explicit criteria, measure, and turn it back on. Self-reported confidence and "be conservative" do not solve it.
feedbacks: Correct. A category with many false positives erodes trust in the good categories. Turn it off, refine the explicit criterion, measure, and turn it back on.
Tempting because it filters out the noise. But self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the filter would be arbitrary and could cut security findings.
Tempting because it is minimal. But it is a vague criterion ("conservative"), which produces inconsistent results instead of precision.
Tempting because it seems robust. But it is more complex, doubles the cost, and does not fix the criterion that generates the noise.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, a C# script uses the Messages API directly (manual loop) to generate tests: it calls the model, executes the requested tools, and ends the loop when the response text contains "done". In some runs, the loop ends with a tool call still pending; in others, it never ends. What is the fix?
opcoes: End the loop after a fixed number of 10 iterations, which is enough in most cases.
Replace the keyword with a rarer marker, such as "<<END>>", and instruct the model to use it.
Decide by stop_reason: tool_use → execute and return tool_result; end_turn → stop; handle max_tokens and the others.
End the loop whenever the response contains any text block.
questoes.explicacao: An agentic loop is controlled by stop_reason (tool_use → continue; end_turn → stop). Text and fixed limits are not the stopping mechanism.
feedbacks: Tempting because it guarantees termination. But a fixed limit as the primary mechanism cuts off legitimate runs and does not solve the premature termination; it only serves as a backstop.
Tempting because it reduces text-based false positives. But it still decides the loop based on natural language; the response may contain the marker alongside a tool_use.
Correct. stop_reason is the loop's control signal. Having text in the response does not mean it is finished: content can mix text and tool_use.
Tempting because text looks like a final answer. But content can mix text and tool_use; that is exactly the case of ending with a pending tool.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the test generation job runs with -p --max-turns 3 and ends with a limit error in 40% of runs, without complete tests. A colleague proposes raising it to --max-turns 50 and calling it done. What is the most appropriate approach?
opcoes: Remove the turn limit entirely, since the model knows when it is done.
Keep --max-turns 3 and accept the partial tests, to preserve the cost.
Wrap the command in a shell loop that reruns the whole job until dotnet test passes, with --max-turns 3 on each run to keep each round cheap.
Use a generous --max-turns only as a backstop, with an explicit done criterion in the prompt (target tests passing), overruns as a visible failure, and --max-budget-usd for cost.
questoes.explicacao: --max-turns is a backstop; termination comes from the model with an explicit done criterion. Exceeding the limit must be a visible failure; cost is controlled with a budget cap.
feedbacks: Tempting because the model does in fact decide when to stop. But without any backstop, an anomalous run can keep going and spending indefinitely in CI.
Tempting because of the cost ceiling. But it uses the limit as the primary stopping mechanism and delivers incomplete work in 40% of runs.
Tempting because it pursues the result. But each rerun starts from scratch, multiplies the cost, and has no stopping criterion other than success.
Correct. An iteration limit is a backstop, not the primary mechanism. An explicit completion criterion and a cost cap (--max-budget-usd) protect the pipeline without cutting off legitimate runs.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the test generation job uses an internal MCP tool, coverage_by_file. When the coverage report has not yet been generated by the previous step, the tool responds "Operation failed". In these cases, Claude has started inventing plausible percentages and generated tests for files that were already covered. What is the best fix in the tool?
opcoes: Make the tool return 0% coverage when the report does not exist, so that Claude keeps generating tests instead of stalling the job in the middle of the pipeline.
Return a structured error: isError, category (missing prerequisite), isRetryable false, the attempted action, and guidance to generate the coverage first.
Instruct in the prompt: "if the tool fails, do not make up values".
Automatically repeat the call 5 times with exponential backoff before returning the error.
questoes.explicacao: A generic error ("Operation failed") is an anti-pattern. Structured error: category, retryable or not, attempted action, and guidance. Retry is only for transient errors.
feedbacks: Tempting because it keeps the flow moving. But it turns a failure into false data: it is silent error suppression, and the files that were already covered would receive duplicate tests.
Correct. The structured error says what failed, whether retrying helps, and what to do. That way Claude can reason about recovery instead of improvising.
Tempting because it targets the fabrication. But it does not give Claude the information needed to recover, and it remains probabilistic; the cause is the generic error.
Tempting because retry is the standard response to failures. But the missing report is not a transient failure: repeating does not create the file, it only delays the same error.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, leadership has approved having PRs classified as "low risk" (documentation or tests only) automatically approved by Claude. "Medium" and "high" risk PRs still get human review. Internal audit wants continuous quality control over the automated decisions and the classifications. Which design is most appropriate?
opcoes: Risk-stratified sampling: larger fractions in the higher-risk tiers and a smaller, but never zero, fraction among the auto-approved.
Uniform sampling of 5% of all PRs, regardless of risk.
Audit only the PRs in which Claude reports confidence below 0.7 in its own classification.
Skip auditing the auto-approved PRs, since only documentation and test PRs fall into that tier, and audit 100% of the high-risk PRs.
questoes.explicacao: Human review: risk-stratified sampling (including the automated tier), neither uniform nor driven by self-reported confidence.
feedbacks: Correct. Stratified sampling concentrates human effort where errors cost more, without leaving the automated tier unverified.
Tempting because of its statistical simplicity. But it spends the same review effort where the risk is different, and it may sample very few cases from the critical tiers.
Tempting because it focuses on the doubtful cases. But self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated: a confident error would never be audited.
Tempting because the tier seems harmless. But the risk classification can also be wrong: a misclassified PR would reach production without any human eyes on it.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, the dashboard shows that the automated review has 92% precision (findings accepted by the devs). Even so, the platform team says the comments on the Terraform files in infra/ "are almost all wrong". What is the correct next step?
opcoes: Trust the aggregate number, since 92% is above the 85% target.
Permanently exclude infra/ from the automated review and keep the other directories as they are, since the overall average is good.
Break down precision by directory and finding category, with a detected_pattern field on each finding.
Increase the review effort for all files.
questoes.explicacao: Aggregate metrics hide per-segment failures. Break them down by type/directory/category and use detected_pattern to measure which patterns generate dismissed findings.
feedbacks: Tempting because the target was met. But an aggregate metric can mask a failure concentrated in one segment; the complaint is specific and measurable.
Tempting because it eliminates the complaint. But it decides without measuring: it may discard useful findings, and it does not reveal which pattern generates the errors.

Correct. Measure before changing anything: the per-segment breakdown reveals whether infra/ has low precision hidden by the average, and detected_pattern points to which rule needs a better criterion.
Tempting because more effort seems like more quality. But it acts without a diagnosis, makes every PR more expensive, and may not even touch the cause.

questoes.pergunta: At Rota Viva, to diagnose failing integration tests, the job passes Claude the full execution log (about 15 MB of build output, warnings, and traces) followed by the question. The analyses come back vague and sometimes ignore the failure that appears in the middle of the log. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Use a model with a larger context window so that the entire log fits without cuts.
Preprocess the log: extract only the failed tests (message, stack trace, neighboring lines) and put that at the beginning of the prompt.
Repeat the question at the beginning and end of the prompt, keeping the entire log in the middle.
Split the log into 30 parts and send each one in a Batch API request.
questoes.explicacao: Trim tool output/logs down to what is relevant and put the key findings at the beginning; a larger window does not solve "lost in the middle".
feedbacks: Tempting because the log is large. But fitting is not the same as being used: "lost in the middle" persists, and the cost per run rises sharply.
Correct. Trim the output to what is relevant and put the essentials at the beginning: less noise, and nothing critical lost in the middle.
Tempting because it helps keep the task in mind. But the problem is that the failure is buried in 15 MB of noise; repeating the question does not bring the evidence any closer.
Tempting because of the batch savings. But it fragments the context (the failure may depend on lines in different parts) and introduces up to 24h of waiting into a CI diagnosis.

questoes.pergunta:
SCENARIO — Lume Comex is a digital customs broker based in Santos that processes ~40,000 documents per month for importers: commercial invoices, packing lists, and bills of lading (B/L), as native or scanned PDFs, in Portuguese, English, and Chinese. A pipeline with Claude extracts the data into a JSON that feeds the ERP and the pre-filling of the import declaration. Constraints: the amounts must reconcile (line items × total, weights across documents); the tax classification code (NCM) has 8 digits; no data may be invented; there is a month-end peak; and human customs brokers review whatever the system cannot guarantee.

Problem: today the prompt ends with "return the answer in JSON" and the code parses the text. In ~3% of documents the parse fails (trailing comma, text before the JSON) or required fields are missing. What is the most appropriate fix?
opcoes: Add to the prompt a complete example of the expected JSON, with all fields, and the sentence "do not write anything outside the JSON".
Prefill the assistant response with "{" to force the JSON to start.
Use structured outputs (output_config.format with json_schema) or an extraction tool with strict: true.
Create a repair routine that fixes commas and removes any text before "{" prior to parsing.
questoes.explicacao: Free text can come out malformed or incomplete. To guarantee the shape: structured outputs (output_config.format) or a tool with input_schema + strict: true.
feedbacks: Tempting because it usually reduces failures. But it is still probabilistic: it improves the rate but guarantees neither syntax nor fields.
Tempting because it used to be a well-known technique. But it guarantees neither fields nor types, and on the newer models assistant prefill is not accepted.
Correct. With structured outputs, or with a tool whose input_schema is the desired output and strict: true, the response follows the schema: valid JSON, with the expected fields and types.
Tempting because it solves some of the cases. But it only addresses syntax; missing fields or fields with the wrong type still get through.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the commercial invoice extraction schema has the incoterm field as a required string with enum ["EXW","FOB","CFR","CIF","DAP","DDP"]. Many invoices do not state the incoterm, and the audit found that, in these cases, the system frequently records "FOB". What is the fix?
opcoes: Make the field nullable (string or null) and instruct the model to return null when the incoterm is not explicitly stated.
Keep the field required and add "do not make up the incoterm" to the prompt.
Retry the extraction until the incoterm is found.
Set FOB as the default value in code when the field comes back empty, since it is the most common incoterm in Lume's importer portfolio.
questoes.explicacao: Data that may be missing → nullable field (null), neither required nor with an invented default. Consider an enum with "other"/"unclear" when applicable.
feedbacks: Correct. A required, non-nullable field forces the model to pick some value when the data does not exist. With null allowed, absence is recorded as absence.
Tempting because it targets the fabrication. But the schema still requires a value from the enum; the instruction fights the structure, and the structure wins.
Tempting because retries fix errors. But a retry does not recover information that is not in the source; the result would be another guess.
Tempting because it reflects the statistics. But it is the system itself inventing the data, with a tax impact (the tax calculation base).

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, extraction already uses structured outputs with the complete schema, and 100% of the responses are valid JSON. Even so, in ~4% of invoices the extracted total_amount does not match the sum of quantity × unit_price across the line items, and in some cases the shipment date is earlier than the invoice issue date. What is the best approach?
opcoes: Enable strict: true on the auxiliary tools as well, because that guarantees the values are correct.
Add "check the sums before answering" to the prompt and trust the result.
Automatically discard invoices with discrepancies between line items and total or with inconsistent dates, and ask the importer to resend the corrected document.
Validate the semantic rules in code (sum of the line items, order of the dates), extracting both the stated and the calculated total, and resend the specific errors.
questoes.explicacao: Valid schema ≠ correct data. Semantic validation in code (sums, dates, contradictions), with stated vs. calculated values and a retry guided by the errors.
feedbacks: Tempting because of the word "strict". But strict guarantees schema conformance (fields and types), not semantic consistency between values.
Tempting because it is cheap. But it is a probabilistic check, without any deterministic verification of the output.
Tempting because it is conservative. But many of the discrepancies are recoverable extraction errors; discarding them causes rework and delays customs clearance.
Correct. Schema conformance is not semantic correctness. Validate in code; extracting both the stated and the calculated values exposes the discrepancy, and the specific errors feed the retry.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the team is going to implement the validation-and-retry loop for invoice extraction. Which two practices are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: On the new attempt, return the specific errors to the model (field, rule violated, value obtained, and value expected).
Repeat the same call, with no changes to the prompt, until validation passes, since the model's sampling varies on each run.
Retry until the gross weight appears when it is missing from the invoice, because the field is required in the ERP.
Set a maximum number of attempts and, once it is exhausted, route the document to human review with the remaining errors.
Increase the effort on each attempt, starting at low, to save on the ones that pass on the first try.
questoes.explicacao: Loop: extract → validate → return specific errors → retry up to a limit → fail with an error/human review. A retry does not create missing data.
