feedbacks: Correct. A retry only improves things if the model knows exactly what to fix; specific errors guide the correction.
Tempting because it sometimes passes. But without feedback it is a blind attempt, it is expensive, and it has no stopping criterion.
Tempting because the ERP requires the field. But a retry does not recover information that is not in the source; the right answer is null and routing, not insistence.
Correct. The loop needs to end: after the limit, fail explicitly and route to a human with the diagnosis.
Tempting because of the savings. But it does not replace error feedback; without knowing what to fix, more effort does not lead to the right answer.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, packing lists from Chinese suppliers have columns such as "数量 (件)" and "箱数", and sometimes "PCS/CTN". The model frequently confuses quantity per carton with the total quantity of pieces. The prose instruction already explains the difference. What is the most effective improvement?
opcoes: Automatically translate all documents into Portuguese before extraction.
Include 2 to 4 varied examples of these layouts (one with PCS/CTN), with the excerpt, the correct extraction, and the reasoning.
Include 15 examples of simple packing lists in English, to give the model more grounding.
Repeat the prose explanation in bold and with "ATTENTION".
questoes.explicacao: Ambiguous formats in extraction → 2–4 varied examples that cover the edge cases, with input, output, and reasoning.
feedbacks: Tempting because it removes the language barrier. But the confusion is about column semantics (per carton vs. total), not language; translation may even make the ambiguity worse.
Correct. Few-shot examples targeted at the ambiguous formats, with reasoning, teach the interpretation pattern and reduce extraction errors.
Tempting because more examples seem better. But examples that do not cover the ambiguous case do not teach the distinction, and the volume increases cost and the risk of literal imitation.
Tempting because the instruction exists and simply "went unnoticed". But the prose has already failed; the model needs a concrete demonstration, not emphasis.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the team marked the register_invoice tool with strict: true; its input_schema has a root object and an items array of objects. The request is rejected with a schema validation error. The root declares additionalProperties: false, but the objects inside items do not. Some fields (e.g., notes) are not in required. What is the fix?
opcoes: Remove strict: true, since extraction worked without it.
Put all fields in required, including notes, because strict mode does not accept optional properties.
Declare additionalProperties: false on the objects in items as well (and on any other nested object).
Replace the items array with a string containing the items serialized as CSV.
questoes.explicacao: strict/structured outputs: every object needs additionalProperties: false (including nested ones). Optional properties are accepted, within a limit.
feedbacks: Tempting because it makes the error go away. But it gives up the guarantee that the tool inputs follow the schema, which was the reason for enabling it.
Tempting because it is a common belief. But strict accepts optional properties (there is a limit on how many); what it requires is additionalProperties: false on every object.
Correct. In strict/structured outputs, every object in the schema, including nested ones, must declare additionalProperties: false.
Tempting because it eliminates the nested object. But it destroys the structure that was meant to be guaranteed and pushes parsing into an unvalidated string.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the strict extraction schema includes "quantity" with minimum: 1, "description" with maxLength: 120, and "net_weight", which can never be greater than "gross_weight". The team expects strict to guarantee these three rules. Which statement is correct?
opcoes: Just enable strict: true; the three rules become guaranteed by schema-constrained generation, with no need for subsequent validation.
Only the weight rule needs code; minimum and maxLength are guaranteed by strict.
Validate all three in code (feeding the retry): strict guarantees structure and types, not ranges, lengths, or relationships between fields.
Change the schema to use oneOf with the valid combinations, which strict is able to guarantee.
questoes.explicacao: strict does not support numeric ranges (minimum/maximum), string length (minLength/maxLength), or recursion (oneOf is not even listed as supported), and cross-field rules cannot be expressed in the schema. Enforce these in code.
feedbacks: Tempting because strict "guarantees the schema". But numeric and string-length constraints are not supported in strict mode, and a cross-field rule cannot even be expressed in plain JSON Schema.
Tempting because the cross-field rule is the one most clearly outside the schema. But minimum and maxLength are also among the constraints not supported in strict mode.
Correct. strict covers a subset of JSON Schema: structure, types, required, enums. Ranges, lengths, and cross-field rules belong in your validation code.
Tempting because oneOf seems to express rules. But it is not among the supported constructs, and combinations of numeric values could not be enumerated that way.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the extraction agent was given 14 tools: OCR, language detection, NCM lookup, currency conversion, importer registry lookup, three ERP write tools, email sending, and ticket creation, among others. The agent has started choosing the wrong tools (e.g., writing to the ERP before validating the NCM). The descriptions have already been rewritten, with little improvement. What is the best change?
opcoes: Rewrite the descriptions once more, this time with usage examples for each tool.
Split into specialized agents (extraction, tax validation, integration) under a coordinator, each with 4 or 5 tools.
Merge all the tools into a single one, execute_action, with a type parameter that selects the operation, reducing the catalog to a single entry.
Spell out in the system prompt the exact order in which the tools must be called.
questoes.explicacao: Guideline: 4–5 tools per agent at decision time. With a large catalog, split into specialized agents (or use tool search); better descriptions alone do not solve it.
feedbacks: Tempting because the description is the selection criterion. But that has already been done with little improvement; with 14 tools, improving the descriptions alone is not enough.
Correct. With too many tools visible at decision time, selection degrades even with good descriptions. Specialized agents keep few tools per decision.
Tempting because it reduces the number of tools. But it just hides the choice inside a parameter, with an even more generic description; the selection problem remains, now less visible.
Tempting because the order is known. But it is a probabilistic prompt for something that should be structural, and it does not reduce the tool overload.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the flow for each document is always the same: classify the type (invoice, packing list, B/L) → extract the fields with that type's schema → validate → write to the ERP. The steps and their order are known and do not change from one document to another. Which architecture is most appropriate?
opcoes: Prompt chaining: one stage per step, with the right schema per type and validation in code between stages.
An autonomous agent with all the tools, which decides for each document which steps to execute.
A multi-agent coordinator that dynamically creates subtasks based on the content of each document.
A single prompt that classifies, extracts, validates, and formats the write all at once, to reduce latency and the number of calls per document.
questoes.explicacao: Fixed, known steps → prompt chaining with programmatic validation between stages. Dynamic decomposition is for open-ended problems.
feedbacks: Correct. Fixed, sequential steps known in advance are the case for prompt chaining: each stage has a focused prompt, and code controls the transitions.
Tempting because of the flexibility. But the flow is fixed; giving the model the decision of which steps to follow adds variability and risk with no benefit.
Tempting because it is sophisticated. But dynamic decomposition is for open-ended investigation; here it is unnecessary complexity.
Tempting because of the simplicity. But it mixes tasks, prevents a type-specific schema, and hides where each failure happens.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the agent's system prompt says: "only call write_to_erp if the total reconciles with the line items and all NCMs have 8 valid digits". An audit found 11 writes in one month that violated the rule and led to amended tax filings. What is the appropriate fix?
opcoes: Reinforce the system prompt with examples of documents that must not be written.
Ask the agent to confirm the validations in writing ("total reconciled: yes; NCMs valid: yes") before each ERP write call.
Run a weekly audit that detects and reverses the improper writes.
A prerequisite in code (PreToolUse hook or a check in the tool) that validates the total and the NCMs and blocks write_to_erp if they fail.
questoes.explicacao: Critical rule (financial/tax) → programmatic enforcement (hook/prerequisite). A prompt is best-effort.
feedbacks: Tempting because examples help the model. But it is still a prompt; with tax consequences, a non-zero failure rate is unacceptable.
Tempting because it makes the reasoning explicit. But the model can claim to have validated without having done so; it is self-assessment, not a guarantee.
Tempting because it is a control. But it acts after the damage (the amendments have already happened).
Correct. A rule with financial or tax consequences goes into deterministic code: the write simply does not happen if the validations fail, and the agent receives the reason so it can recover.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, when a document exhausts its extraction attempts, it goes to the customs brokers' queue with only the message "extraction failed". The brokers redo everything from scratch, which takes ~25 minutes per document. What is the best improvement to the handoff?
opcoes: Attach to the queue the full transcript of all the model's attempts, so that the broker has access to absolutely everything that was done.
Send a structured summary: document, fields already validated, fields that failed (rule and value found), attempts, and recommended action.
Send only the model's overall confidence score for the document, to prioritize the queue.
Increase the maximum number of attempts to reduce the number of documents that reach humans.
questoes.explicacao: Human handoff = structured summary (what was done, what failed and why, values found, recommended action), not a transcript or a generic message.
feedbacks: Tempting because it hides nothing. But the broker would have to read long transcripts to find what matters; the handoff needs to be summarized and structured.
Correct. The human usually does not see the transcript; the structured summary lets them continue from where the system stopped, instead of starting over.
Tempting because it helps order the queue. But self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and it does not tell the broker what to check.
Tempting because it reduces the volume. But many cases are missing information at the source (a retry does not create data), and the poor handoff continues for whatever is left.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the tax validation agent requests, in a single response, three lookup_ncm calls (one for each line item). The code executes all three, but builds the next request with three user messages, each with one tool_result, and the API rejects the request. One of the lookups failed due to a timeout. How should the code return the results?
opcoes: Return only the tool_result of the first call and let the model request the others again.
Omit the lookup that failed and return only the two successful ones, so as not to confuse the model.
Return the three tool_results in a single user message, each with its tool_use_id; the timed-out one with is_error: true.
Repeat the failed lookup until it succeeds, and only then return the three results.
questoes.explicacao: Parallel tool use: all tool_results in a single user message, each with its tool_use_id; failures with is_error: true.
feedbacks: Tempting because it simplifies things. But every pending tool_use needs a corresponding tool_result; leaving calls unanswered breaks the protocol.
Tempting because it hides the noise. But it is silent suppression: the failed tool_use is left without a result, and the model does not know it needs to recover.
Correct. In parallel tool use, all results go in a single user message, each referencing the exact tool_use_id; the failure also gets a result, with is_error: true.
Tempting because it delivers everything complete. But without a limit it can hang the flow; a persistent timeout should go back to the model as an error so that it can decide.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, the dashboard shows 97% per-field accuracy. When reviewing a sample, the brokers noticed that on scanned B/Ls with handwritten annotations, the accuracy for weight and container number is around 60%. Leadership wants to reduce human review. Which two actions are most appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Keep review by uniform sampling of 5% of all documents, since the average is high.
Break down accuracy by document type, origin (native or scanned), and field, to locate where extraction fails.
Waive human review for the fields in which the model reports confidence above 0.9, focusing the brokers on the rest.
Raise the acceptance threshold for all documents from 97% to 99%.
Risk-stratified sampling: review scanned and high-value B/Ls more, and stable native PDFs less.
questoes.explicacao: Break metrics down by document type and field (the aggregate masks failures) and use risk-stratified sampling, neither uniform nor driven by self-reported confidence.
feedbacks: Tempting because of the simplicity. But uniform sampling dilutes the review of handwritten B/Ls, precisely where the failure is concentrated.
Correct. An aggregate accuracy of 97% can hide 60% in one segment; breaking it down by type and field shows where to focus effort.
Tempting because it reduces review. But uncalibrated self-reported confidence means nothing; confident errors would slip straight through.
Tempting because it is more demanding. But it changes a global number without addressing the problem segment, and the aggregate metric keeps hiding the failure.
Correct. Risk-stratified sampling focuses human review where errors are more likely or more costly, freeing up the stable segments.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, for the same shipment, the commercial invoice states a gross weight of 1,250 kg and the packing list states 1,310 kg. The pipeline needs to generate the consolidated JSON for pre-filling the declaration. How should the discrepancy be handled?
opcoes: Record both values with the source of each (document and page), flag the discrepancy, and route it to the customs broker.
Use the average, 1,280 kg, since it is the most likely value.
Always use the value from the commercial invoice, the document with the greatest legal weight in customs clearance, and discard the packing list value.
Use the higher value, since it is the most conservative for freight purposes.
questoes.explicacao: Provenance: in a conflict, annotate the conflicting values with their sources and flag it. Never choose silently or take the average.
feedbacks: Correct. In a conflict between sources, preserve the conflicting values with provenance and flag it; do not silently pick one or take the average.
Tempting because it seems neutral. But the average is a number that no document states, with an impact on freight and taxes.
Tempting because there is an apparent hierarchy. But it chooses silently and hides the discrepancy, which may indicate a shipping error and needs to be seen.
Tempting because it sounds prudent. But it still chooses silently, and the "conservative" criterion may be wrong for tax purposes.

questoes.pergunta: At Lume Comex, to reduce review, the team wants the model to return a per-field confidence and to automatically approve fields with confidence ≥ 0.9. Before putting this into production, what is indispensable?
opcoes: Ask the model, in the prompt, to be rigorous when assigning the confidences.
Use a second model to provide the confidence, instead of the extraction model itself.
Apply the 0.9 threshold right away and monitor complaints from importers.
Calibrate the per-field confidence against a labeled set and set the thresholds per field and document type based on that.
questoes.explicacao: Per-field confidence is only useful if it is calibrated against a labeled set; without that, the threshold is arbitrary.
feedbacks: Tempting because it is simple. But "be rigorous" is a vague criterion and does not make self-reported confidence any better calibrated.
Tempting because it separates the roles. But the second model's confidence also needs to be calibrated; changing who reports it does not solve the problem.
Tempting because of the agility. But it uses customers as the error detector for tax data; the damage happens before the measurement.
Correct. Confidence only has meaning if it is calibrated against labeled data; the thresholds must come from measurement per field and per segment.
